name: Automated face recognition
definition: Cameras and computers that identify people by matching their faces against stored images.

milestones2.what: Takeo Kanade publicly demonstrated a face-matching system that located facial features and measured ratios without human intervention.

sources.title: Facial recognition system
sources.quote: In 1970, Takeo Kanade publicly demonstrated a face-matching system that located anatomical features such as the chin

milestones2.note: Bledsoe, Chan and Bisson (1964-65) needed a human to mark feature coordinates, so rejected as semi-automated; the earlier system did the matching by computer, so a looser reading would date the demonstration to 1964-65.

milestones2.what: The Bochum face-recognition system, by 1997 outperforming other systems, was sold commercially as ZN-Face to operators of airports and other busy locations.

sources.title: Facial recognition system
sources.quote: was sold commercially on the market as ZN-Face to operators of airports and other busy locations.

milestones2.note: Earlier than Mexico 2000. The same article says West Virginia and New Mexico DMVs were first to use automated face recognition after 1993 (search results say West Virginia from 1998), but no dated source was fetchable. 1997 comes from ZN-Face commercial sale to airports, so it is a rough date.

milestones2.what: Apple announced Face ID on the iPhone X, bringing face recognition to ordinary phone unlocking.

sources.title: Face ID
sources.quote: Apple announced Face ID alongside the iPhone X on September 12, 2017

milestones2.note: Introduction date, not a measured adoption figure.
milestones2.check_note: Introduction date, not a measured adoption figure. Earlier face-unlock phones (e.g. Android 4.0 Face Unlock, 2011) were niche and unreliable. Kept.

name: Speech synthesis
definition: A machine that generates spoken language with an artificial voice, such as a talking computer reading out answers.

milestones2.what: Wolfgang von Kempelen's bellows-operated acoustic-mechanical speech machine, with models of tongue and lips producing vowels and consonants, described in a 1791 paper.

sources.title: Speech synthesis
sources.quote: There followed the bellows-operated "acoustic-mechanical speech machine" of Wolfgang von Kempelen of Pressburg, Hungary, described in a 1791 paper.

sources.title: Wolfgang von Kempelen
sources.quote: Kempelen also created a manually operated speaking machine.

milestones2.note: Date is the publication of his description; he worked on the machine for about twenty years before, so a working demonstration probably came earlier (the same page gives 1789 for his book, so sources conflict). Earlier candidate: Kratzenstein 1779, vocal-tract models producing five vowels only, rejected as not producing speech. Later: Voder 1939 (first electronic, human-operated, shown at the New York World's Fair), Kelly-Gerstman IBM 7090 computer synthesis 1961, Umeda's English text-to-speech 1968. The machine was hand-operated, as was the Voder.

milestones2.what: Telesensory Systems' Speech+ talking calculator for the blind, with a synthesized voice, was in use; the Kurzweil Reading Machine for the Blind (Votrax synthesizer) appeared in the same year.

sources.title: Speech synthesis
sources.quote: One of the first was the Telesensory Systems Inc. (TSI) Speech+ portable calculator for the blind in 1976.

milestones2.note: Earlier systems existed (Umeda's 1968 text-to-speech, MUSA 1975 reading Italian) but I found no evidence they were used outside the lab. Voder (1939) and Kempelen's machine were exhibitions. Date 1976 is the source's year for 'one of the first' handheld devices; a slightly earlier use is possible.
milestones2.check_note: Rechecked: Votrax VS4 (1971-73), Unix speak (1972-74), MUSA 1975 were lab or commercial components with no documented end use; Kurzweil Reading Machine (Votrax-based) is the same era. 1976 confirmed on the evidence available. Prior: Earlier systems existed (Umeda's 1968 text-to-speech, MUSA 1975 reading Italian) but I found no evidence they were used outside the lab. Voder (1939) and Kempelen's machine were exhibitions. Date 1976 is the source's year for 'one of the first' handheld devices; a slightly earlier use is possible.

milestones2.what: Siri on the iPhone 4S brought a talking computer that answers aloud to ordinary phone users.

sources.title: Siri
sources.quote: On October 14, 2011, Apple launched the iPhone 4S with a beta version of Siri.

milestones2.note: Judgment call. Earlier mass-market talking devices: Texas Instruments Speak & Spell (1978) and talking games and chess computers (1979-80), which had voices but little routine use as 'answering computers'. Wikipedia source supports the date of launch, not the synthesis itself.

name: Companion or sex robot
definition: A robot built to provide companionship, affection, romance or sex.

milestones2.what: Sony introduced the first consumer AIBO robot dog (ERS-110)

sources.title: AIBO
sources.quote: The first consumer model was introduced on 11 May 1999 and was followed by updated generations.

milestones2.note: Companionship fit is loose (AIBO means pal). Paro was designed from 1993 but first shown to the public in late 2001 per the page read (first pass said 1998, not confirmed). No romance or sex robot (RealDoll 1997 is a doll, not a robot; Realbotix 2018) earlier.
milestones2.check_note: Earlier: Elektro/Sparko 1939-40 are exhibits, Paro designed from 1993 but first public in 2001, Furby 1998 is a toy creature not a companion. No earlier robot built for companionship found. Companionship fit of AIBO is loose.

milestones2.what: AIBO ERS-110 went on sale and sold out in 20 minutes

sources.title: AIBO
sources.quote: Sales began on 1 June 1999 and sold out via the Internet in 20 minutes.

milestones2.note: Paro handmade versions sold from 2004 are later.
milestones2.check_note: Earlier: Paro handmade sales from 2004, Furby 1998 is a pet toy, not marketed as companion robot; no earlier sale of a companion robot found.

name: Three-dimensional holographic display
definition: A display that shows images, maps or people as volumetric three-dimensional pictures viewable from several sides.

milestones2.what: First practical optical holograms recording 3D objects made by Denisyuk (USSR) and by Leith and Upatnieks (Michigan), viewable from several angles

sources.title: Holography
sources.quote: the first practical optical holograms that recorded 3D objects to be made in 1962 by Yuri Denisyuk in the Soviet Union

milestones2.note: Static holograms are a loose match for a 'display'. Other candidates: 1966 varifocal-mirror volumetric display (Volumetric display page), 1972 moving white-light hologram (Lloyd Cross), 1989 MIT electroholographic video display. Perspecta (2001) rejected as late. Gabor 1947-48 holography produced no 3D display.

milestones2.what: Lloyd Cross produced a hologram recreating a moving 3-dimensional image (Multiplex hologram, viewable around a cylinder)

sources.title: Holographic display
sources.quote: 1972 - Lloyd Cross produced the first traditional hologram by using white-light transmission holography to recreate a moving 3-dimensional image.

milestones2.note: 1989 MIT electroholography is a lab system, not practical use. The 1972 Cross moving-image hologram is the earliest fetched 3D hologram display shown to the public (holography art exhibitions from 1968, per Wikipedia Holography, are static plates). Judgement call: practical use is thin, so low.

doubt: Stretch: static holograms (1962) as a 3D display.
search_hints: Decide whether static holograms fit; search for the first display of changing (moving) 3D images viewable without glasses.

name: Machine learning
definition: A machine that improves its performance from experience or data instead of being explicitly programmed for each task.

milestones2.what: Marvin Minsky and Dean Edmonds built SNARC at Princeton (funding summer 1951), a neural-net machine that learned by reinforcement to solve a maze.

sources.title: Stochastic neural analog reinforcement calculator
sources.quote: They tested the machine on a copy of Shannon's maze, and found that it could learn to solve the maze.

milestones2.note: Candidates: Ashby's Homeostat (1948, adapts to disturbances; closer to self-regulation than learning from experience), Shannon's Theseus maze mouse (1950; relays remember the maze path, and whether it 'learned' is disputed), Samuel's checkers program (begun 1949, first ran 1952, paper 1959; 'machine learning' coined 1959) and Rosenblatt's perceptron (1957-58). SNARC is a simulated maze solved by reinforced weights, so I take it as the earliest clear case, but this is a judgment and the date is only the year. Page for Theseus could not be fetched. No first_practical_use or mass_adoption given: ADALINE (1960) adaptive filters and later uses were not sourced, and 'routine' consumer use is too diffuse to date.

name: 3D printing
definition: A machine that builds solid objects automatically from a digital design by adding material layer by layer.

milestones2.what: Hideo Kodama (Nagoya Municipal Industrial Research Institute) published methods and results for building 3D plastic models layer by layer from photo-hardening polymer.

sources.title: 3D printing
sources.quote: His research results as journal papers were published in April and November 1981.

sources.title: 3D printing
sources.quote: In April 1980, Hideo Kodama of Nagoya Municipal Industrial Research Institute invented two additive methods for fabricating three-dimensional plastic models

milestones2.note: Earlier than Hull's 1984 patent. Raytheon 1982 layered-powder patent is later. Whether Kodama's design was driven by a digital design file is not stated; fit is on layer-by-layer automatic building.

milestones2.what: 3D Systems, co-founded by Chuck Hull, commercialised stereolithography (first machine, SLA-1, reported 1987).

sources.title: Stereolithography
sources.quote: After the patent was granted in 1986, Hull co-founded the world's first 3D printing company, 3D Systems, to commercialize it.

milestones2.note: Quote supports commercialisation after 1986 only; the 1987 SLA-1 date comes from the first pass and was not fetched. No mass_adoption established (consumer RepRap era 2005+ not sourced as routine use).

name: Real-time computerized situation display
definition: A computer-driven screen or plotting board that shows the live positions of ships, aircraft or objects tracked by radar and sensors.

milestones2.what: Bedford, MA test: radar data sent by phone line to a computer, displaying a mock enemy aircraft detection (Whirlwind)

sources.title: Semi-Automatic Ground Environment
sources.quote: data produced by a radar was transmitted through telephone lines to a computer for the first time, showing the detection of a mock enemy aircraft.

milestones2.note: Other candidates: DATAR (Royal Canadian Navy/Ferranti, trial late 1953 on Lake Ontario, displays on plan-position indicators), Cape Cod System tests from Sept 1953, Royal Navy CDS (analog, 1940s). 1951 is earliest found.

milestones2.what: SAGE New York sector became operational, direction-center consoles showing radar tracks from the computer

sources.title: Semi-Automatic Ground Environment
sources.quote: On "June 26, 1958,…the New York sector became operational"

milestones2.note: First pass said 1958-07-01 at McGuire AFB; fetched page gives 26 June 1958 for New York sector. DATAR was not fielded; CDS-based Royal Navy ADA later.

name: Computer-run space station
definition: A computer that runs the life support, systems and operations of a space station or colony.

milestones2.what: Skylab launched with an onboard digital computer controlling its attitude and pointing.

sources.title: Skylab
sources.quote: The mission computer used aboard Skylab was the IBM System/4Pi TC-1, a relative of the AP-101 Space Shuttle computers.

sources.title: Skylab
sources.quote: Skylab was launched on May 14, 1973, by the modified Saturn V.

milestones2.note: Sources show an onboard computer for attitude control only, not life support. Salyut 1 (1971) computers not found in fetchable sources, so an earlier event may exist.
